subsubtopic: CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT'S PROPOSED POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde Government. It says one thing but does another. Take the Throne Speech for instance.
The Speech says: "Environment 2000 will be created to carry out... . national park development", but in practice this Government destroyed a park in Banff to accommodate a former Liberal Cabinet Minister's hotel.
The Speech says: "The Government is to reduce poverty among the aged." But the Government refuses to help needy women between the ages of 50 and 65.
The Speech says: "Extend native rights." And yet it does nothing to relieve poverty on our reservations, where in one case 20 people had to live in a house built for six.
The Speech says: "The Government will make divorce more equitable." During the years of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), morality has gone down the drain; marriage takes second place; and common-law wives are now given privileges not extended to married women.
The Speech talks about building a national partnership for prosperity. In practice this Government attacks the provincial Governments at every turn.
The Speech talks about restraint, yet the Government spent $50 million on compulsory metric.
Like Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, this Liberal Government will die a terrible death, and the sooner the better.

subtopic: DUMPING OF UNITED STATES POTATOES ON BRITISH COLUMBIA MARKET
DUMPING OF UNITED STATES POTATOES ON BRITISH COLUMBIA MARKET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, two days ago the potato farmers of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island won a very important anti-dumping action brought against them by the farmers of
the State of Maine. I wish to congratulate the farmers on their victory over very unjust treatment.
Also, I wish to express the anxiety felt by farmers in other regions of Canada, particularly in British Columbia, anxiety that possibly the success in eastern Canada is going to make the Government less vigilant and dampen the Government's determination to pursue the matter of unjust treatment on the West Coast where the farmers of Washington State are dumping potatoes on the market in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia.
I simply want to take this opportunity to urge the Government to pursue the matter of unjust treatment of the farmers of British Columbia in that marketplace with the same kind of vigour with which it pursued the matter in eastern Canada.

subsubtopic: CERTAIN REMARKS ABOUT QUEBEC MEMBERS
speechtext:
First of all, Madam Speaker, I should like to say that we are glad to see you back in the chair of the House. Secondly, I want to take a few seconds to point out to you that yesterday, in a flight of oratory, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) referred to us as the clowns from Quebec. Once again I cannot let that remark of the Hon. Member for Central Nova go unchallenged. First and foremost, it is important to recall that, in this House and throughout the country, Canadians have been ever respectful of one another during the past century. Unfortunately, the Leader of the Official Opposition has yet to understand that every time he says something about Quebecers or refers to Quebec, he never fails to use the word clowns or to make Quebecers believe that he knew what was going on in my riding when he was more than 1,000 kilometres removed from my hometown of Schefferville. In others words, seeking to woo the electors in English-speaking regions or in other provinces by attacking Quebecers, including snide remarks about the personal life of their representatives, does not reflect the way Canada was built and, more to the point, that is not the type of man Canadians want as Prime Minister.
Madam Speaker, I mention this with the hope that the Hon. Member for Central Nova will appreciate that mutual respect and constructive ideas just might be his stepping stone to becoming an outstanding politician-unless he has already lost

subsubtopic: CHILD CARE PROVISION ACHIEVED IN COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, recently a great victory for women and, indeed, for all workers, was won by the United Auto Workers Local 1325 in Stratford, Ontario. In a major breakthrough in collective bargaining, the union fought for and won recognition of child care as an important service for employees.
The employer, Canadian Fabricated Products, has agreed to put two cents per hour worked by employees into a daycare fund, contributing a total of $935 per week. In order for this project to be successful as a demonstration program it is essential that the federal Government participate in funding.
I wish to congratulate the union for achieving this genuine success story for women in the labour movement. Over 90 per cent of the 1,170 workers at the plant are women, including the local union president, plant chairperson, and the entire bargaining committee.
Once again the labour movement is in the forefront of progressive social change. Medicare pensions and human rights legislation also began as individual clauses in union contracts. NDP Members of Parliament join the labour movement in urging the Government to take the necessary steps to guarantee universal daycare for all parents and children in all communities. We urge the federal Government to follow this example and expand daycare for federal employees.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF ARCHIVAL COLLECTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, for three days we have been hearing horror stories about government spending out of control, and clear examples of the Liberals cooking the books. I would like to focus on this Government neglecting books, a clear violation of Canada's cultural heritage.
In the Auditor General's Report two chapters are devoted to grave concern about the federal Government's lack of attention to our priceless national assets in the National Library and the Public Archives of Canada.
Sir Arthur Doughty, the first Dominion Archivist, said this back in 1924:
Of all national assets, archives are the most precious; they are the gift of one generation to another, and the extent of our care of them marks the extent of our civilization.
The Auditor General warns that not only is security woefully inadequate to protect Canada's cultural treasures; worse, there is totally insufficient funding to protect our national assets from deterioration because they are being maintained in unacceptable temperature and humidity conditions. Surely the Government's spending priorities are entirely out of whack. Only one-half person hour per year has been designated for preservation work in the National Library.
I find utterly incredible the fact that the Government wastes untold hundreds of millions of dollars on its short-term political projects, while Canada's precious national assets succumb to age and lack of proper care.

subsubtopic: COST OF COMPLIANCE WITH GOVERNMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a situation recently came to my attention which demonstrates all too clearly the nightmare of red tape that has been imposed upon small business by the Government.
A businessman in my constituency of Brandon-Souris is a distributor of agricultural machinery repair parts. He has been told that, in order to be exempt from duty charges on the products he imports and sells, he must provide detailed records of every transaction. That means a piece of paperwork for items worth only 25 cents. On top of that, he cannot get a straight answer on whether he has to pay federal sales tax on these items. In addition, some larger dealers who are in the same business but have much greater resources are exempt from the very same regulations which he must meet.
His is a story with a familiar ring. Because of the great amount of record keeping involved in some government programs, many small businesses may be inclined to forget about the regulations and forgo the benefits of the programs. If a company simply cannot comply with the regulations, either the extra cost is passed on to the consumer, or the company must discontinue carrying certain products altogether.
It is abundantly clear to owners of small businesses that the Liberals can offer them nothing but pointless interference and prohibitive regulations. The only hope for the small businesses of this country is that the Liberal Government itself will soon be out of business.

subsubtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF HIGH-TECHNOLOGY-IMPACT ON WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, over the past few months the Government has been trumpeting the benefits of high-technology as a panacea for the economic problems we face. Just recently the Minister of State for
December 14, 1983

Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston) sponsored the Canada Tomorrow Conference at a cost of over half a million dollars, to discuss the possible implementation of high-tech applications in Canadian industry.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House an example of the effects of high-technology applications when undertaken with little consideration of the human costs involved. In Midland, Ontario, on Friday, January 13, Bell Canada will close down an office and displace 15 operators. Of course the company will continue to receive its money from Midland, but it will provide 15 fewer jobs in a community which is already hard strapped. Bell Canada has still not announced whether Clinton, Lindsay, Beaverton, and Peterborough will not also be so blessed by the same benefits of its new high-technology applications.
New technology, imposed without consultation and control by workers and smaller communities, has a potential to impose great human and economic suffering. Government has a responsibility to pass legislation to ensure workers some right of control and adequate notice of new technology, especially as, in the case of Bell, the company that is supposed to be government regulated.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT'S REQUEST FOR ACCESS TO DATA BASE OF KITCHENER CITY COUNCIL

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I did have a chance to discuss the matter with the Member for Kitchener. We discussed the procedure followed by the Department of National Revenue in performing its duties, to ensure that the Income Tax Act is enforced equitably and that each Canadian taxpayer pays his fair share, unlike what the Progressive Conservative Party would like to see. They would prefer to have the Income Tax Act enforced inequitably. Let people who can get away with it defraud the system and let others who have no choice pay more taxes, an
attitude that deliberately ignores the principle of equity that should be applied to all Canadian taxpayers.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):

Moreover, the responsibility of the Department of National Revenue for ensuring that this is done means that we must perform audits. By requesting certain data from public institutions such as municipalities or school boards we are fulfilling our responsibility, which is to check whether each Canadian taxpayer is paying his fair share of income tax.

subsubtopic: LOAN COST CHARGES IMPOSED BY CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. For six weeks in a row the Bank of Canada has posted an increase in its interest rate. This increase is at the expense of farmers and small businesses all across the land. We have learned why this is happening from today's business section of The Globe and Mail. The banks of Canada have posted a record $1.89 billion profit. The Globe and Mail, with its usual perception, explains why this is so, and I would like the Minister to deal with the matter. The article in The Globe and Mail reads:
The way the banks made money in hard times was to widen the spread between what they paid on deposits and received in interest from loans.
In other words, the banks have been over-charging Canadians for money, with excessive interest rates. I would ask the Minister when the Government will produce an interest rate policy that will be favourable to farmers, workers, and small businessmen instead of the banks of Canada.

subsubtopic: LOAN COST CHARGES IMPOSED BY CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would first like to point out to the Hon. Member that, in
Oral Questions
spite of the fact that both in Canada and the United States there has been an increase in bank rates, this has had no impact at all in terms of loans to individuals like the farmers and small businessmen to whom the Hon. Member referred. The prime rate has remained the same as it was in the weeks before, which is 11 per cent, the same level as it is in the United States.
As the Hon. Member knows, we are very much influenced by what is happening in the United States in this regard. We have succeeded, in the last year and a half, in eliminating the former 5 per cent, spread in favour of U.S. rates as compared to Canadian rates. We have brought our prime rate to the same level as that of the United States. We have been successful as a country in compressing any difference between the U.S. and Canadian rates.
[DOT] (U25)
As far as the issue of bank profits is concerned, I have to remind my hon. friend that for 1983 it appears that the return on assets of banks in Canada is expected to be .54 per cent; in 1982 it was .43 per cent, and in 1981 it was .57 per cent. The net interest income, which is a tax equivalent, would make it 2.53 per cent in 1983, 2.50 per cent in 1980, and 2.70 per cent in 1981. In effect, in 1983 we have had a situation where the banks have not been in a better position than they were in 1981 before we were hit by the recession. I should like my friend to bear these figures in mind when he raises the points he has just raised.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I summarized by quoting my favourite source of objective information for what is going on in the Canadian economy, the business section of The Globe and Mail. Whatever the Minister says, he cannot avoid that truth.

Madam Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister a question concerning a particular group that is of special concern, and that is the farmers. The number of bankruptcies in the farm sector has gone up by some 16 per cent in the past year. That is not coincidental to the increase in bank profits. In his submission to the Macdonald Royal Commission, the Minister of Agriculture, speaking about farmers, said that the problem is being made worse by increasing costs, including interest rates. Will the Minister of Finance give some consistency in policy and at least take action where the Minister of Agriculture has promised it, and do something for farmers about the exhorbitant interest rates?

Madam Speaker, the Government has already taken a number of steps under the strong urging and pressures from the very able Minister of Agriculture. We have announced a number of steps in the last

December 14, 1983
Oral Questions
budget, and a number of steps even before the last budget, with regard to assisting farmers.
The fact is that interest rates were indeed very high, but they have come down quite substantially in the last year. We have been able to achieve this because, in spite of the opposition of the New Democratic Party, there has been strong support in the country for reducing inflation, and for the six and five program in particular. This has helped us all around to bring our interest rates down at least to the levels they are in the United States. We have succeeded in doing this in spite of the opposition of the NDP.

Madam Speaker, in spite of what the Minister said, everyone, including farmers, knows that they are experiencing a record number of bankruptcies. As the Minister of Agriculture has pointed out, that has everything to do with the exhorbitant interest rates the banks are charging our farmers.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT REDUCE INTEREST RATES
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT REDUCE INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to come back to the general question of interest rates. The Minister knows that it is not only the New Democratic Party but the Economic Council of Canada, the C.D. Howe Institute, Statistics Canada, the Economic Council of Canada, and all kinds of other groups outside the House of Commons, that have been telling the Minister that, unless we bring down interest rates, the economic recovery that is partially under way will become completely stalled.
Will the Minister live up to the 1980 election campaign promise the Government made to bring down interest rates, so that we can do something about the jobs that are needed so badly in our economy?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT REDUCE INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would remind my hon. friend that indeed interest rates have come down quite significantly in the last year. As a matter of fact, today you can get a consumer loan at as low a level as it has been for the last 25 years, between 11 per cent and 13 per cent. If you had tried to buy a car in 1970 and you went to a bank, you would have had to pay between 11 per cent and 13 per cent on that loan. This is the type of loan you can get today. Therefore, in terms of reduction of interest rates, compared to where they were six months ago, where they were a year ago, and a year and a half ago, there has been a tremendous success in this country. We are going to try to press on with this.
I invite my hon. friend to come out of his dream world and face the real world where we are very interdependent with what is happening in the American economy. That is not only Canada, but it is the fate of all western industrialized countries. This is why, at the Economic Summit at Williamsburg, at the IMF and in the OECD meetings, we have urged, together with other industrialized countries, the American
authorities to do everything they can to bring down real U.S. interest rates.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say at
the outset that I hope you will stay and listen and I hope the Hon. Member on the other side will stay and listen to my comments. May I congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Speech from the Throne for their contribution as colleagues, as Members of Parliament and in bringing to our attention particularly their interest in their responsibilities with this House. May I as well, Mr. Speaker, ask you to pass on to Madam Speaker my personal delight that she is back in good health again and with us. As well, may I congratulate you on a superb job under what I think all sides of the House recognize is a very trying ordeal, to sit in that chair and try to keep this forum under control and within its rules.
I hope today, in the few minutes available to me, to dwell particularly on two areas which are of considerable interest and concern. The first is multiculturalism, a public policy, which if properly approached can do a great deal to bring together the destiny of this nation but, if improperly handled, can indeed help to divide up this very great and very diverse nation of ours. As well, I hope to have a few minutes to talk about a free press, because a truly free press is not free simply because government and Parliament have no control or interest in it. It is only free if indeed it is free from any kind of power which might abuse the intent of giving all Canadians a free flow of information and allowing access for the greatest number of people to the expression of their views.
The Address-Mr. Fleming
If I may, I thought it might be appropriate in this Throne Speech debate, which is allowed to be rather wide-ranging, to make reference to certain much-quoted public criticisms that I have made recently and certainly have become great fodder for our friends opposite in the early days of this Throne Speech debate and the early Question Periods following it. Certainly my comments have been of great interest to that famous Newfoundland tag team, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), whose cohesiveness and support of a common thread in debate is probably much greater in this public forum than I am left with the sense it is in private, and also by the comments made by their Leader himself quoting me as he led off in Question Period the day after the Throne Speech.
I must admit-and with no apology-that I did say the obvious, that the Party of which I am proud to be a part, the Party that is now in Government in our country, is not in very good shape with the Canadian public. We are in a bad position in public opinion polls. I offered, when asked by the press, several reasons why I thought that was so. I said, "Yes, there is in my view too much centralization of power on the bureaucratic side", and I said, "I believe there is a similar problem on the political side currently with the operations of the Government". I said as well-although I must say that in the selective readings of Hon. Members of the Opposition it did not gain any attention-that part of the tragedy of our being seen as having, and perhaps indeed having, too much of what I call cynicism, ballyhoo and manipulation in our operations was that we had some excellent policies which have helped the country and have set it on a positive course. Indeed, we were not getting the credit I thought we deserved for those policies because of some of that cynicism, ballyhoo and manipulation. Lest the selective readings of the Official Opposition leave a misimpression, let me say that we will never, and certainly do not at the current moment, take a back seat to them. They do not take a back seat to us on cynicism, ballyhoo and manipul-tion. I think it is important that things be put in that context. At least we have policies. At least we are prepared to take criticism, because in a country as diverse as our own it is very difficult ever to satisfy all the various parts of Canada, all the various constituencies, at the same time.
However, I think we have much to be proud of in the fact that inflation now, from I believe the most recent statistic, is under 5 per cent. Certainly I know as a Member of Parliament for more than a decade the immense fear in the minds of the public when interest rates went up to the 20 per cent range and inflation was well up into the teens. I am proud of that statistic. It did not happen by accident. Part of it was public policy. Part of it was the six and five program.
Constitutional reform, so much a matter of disruption in the House, is a very important piece of history. I am very pleased to have been a part of that. I am very proud that this Government accomplished that. I must say that the major debate from the other side was not on content but was on form. That is usually the kind of criticism we get from them because they are afraid to take a position on content itself.

December 14, 1983
The Address-Mr. Fleming
Yes, indeed, surely everybody must admit that when the National Energy Program was put together, forecasts of what would happen because of the international oil cartel are not what indeed in time did happen. There is an overabundance of supply in some cases, a selling off of various kinds of oil at lower than the cartel price. That has led to the need for some adjustment to the NEP. However, the Canadianization aspect of that national energy policy is fundamental to the future of the country. I am proud the Government had the guts to put forward that policy and fight it through.
1 am not critical of content. I am not critical of policies. I offer some criticism of the way we are perceived by the public, and I believe that that tells us we will have to do something about it. I do not think it is an original thought on my part. I think my Party in convention about a year ago overwhelmingly endorsed a resolution using the same words I used in my public criticism. From leaked reports of the Party President's reform commission, similar things have been said. Let me say that at least I am proud we have put forward policies. Let me say there is a great danger to the country in too much, on this side of the House and on the Official Opposition side, cynicism, ballyhoo and manipulation rather than hard facts and open discussion. Also let me say that after many years in power there is a danger that one comes to know the tools too well and uses them too well. I find it very frightening that without having power and under this new Leader they have achieved levels of cynicism, ballyhoo and manipulation which frighten me. If we have a problem to clean up over here, they certainly do over there. They operate in that manner without at least something we have on this side-sound policies to put forward and the guts to put forward controversial issues which must be put forward if this country is to be kept on track.
When I talk about cynicism, ballyhoo and manipulation, let me just say of the Hon. Member for St. John's West, who has had such glee in quoting me, that I cannot think of an individual in the House, as much as I find myself enjoying his humour from time to time, who produces more fluff and less stuff per 10,000 decibels. Were Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey in business today, he would vie to be the all-time champ in the centre ring, the ring master-all fluff and no stuff and a master of ballyhoo, buffoonery and bluster. P.T. Barnum would jump up and click his heels. We well remember that when the Hon. Member for St. John's West jumped up and clicked his heels, his mukluks fell off and we had an election.
As far as manipulation is concerned, anyone who followed the saga of the Conservative leadership race knows that manipulation took on a space age meaning during that contest. We read now reports of people being brought out to elect delegates and being paid $10 each. We know of the manipulation of new Canadians, without any explaining to them through language barriers what it was all about, or what the process was, to gain delegate votes. While there were public professions of support for the former Leader by the current Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) behind the scenes, we know now there was a sharpening of many knives and a
great deal of manipulation going on. When I talk about this Party having some problems, thank goodness we do not exercise it quite to the degree they do over there.
Finally, if we have to talk about cynicism and public perceptions, what better source than the current best seller, Contenders: The Tory Quest for Power, wherein Patrick Martin, Allan Gregg and George Perlin quote from a very famous memo, now alleged to have been composed by the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson), who noted in a memo to his leadership candidate, the now Leader of the Opposition, that that person was not trusted because delegates were not certain who he was or what he stood for. They also thought the Leader of the Opposition was an opportunist and believed that people around him were unacceptable. Finally, the memo warned:
Your campaign is a threat. They don't trust you because of the slickness, smoothness ... feeling there is no substance.
The Hon. Leader of the Opposition gave me the Order of Canada, I thank you very much, for my honesty in talking about problems on this side.

The John Thompson referred to in that book is not the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) nor indeed a Member of Parliament at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is right.

I think the content is still very interesting, that a senior organizer for the current Leader of the Opposition said what he said. I simply want to point out, if it does not sound too pious because we all have our warts, that as one member of the House, as one Canadian who has been elected, I think it is in the interests of the Canadian public for political Parties on all sides to do better at bringing forward policies.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member clearly alleged that those comments were made by the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson). They were not, and I insist that he retract those statements immediately.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have been told they were not by him. If they are not by him, I retract. I said I will check. I understand from the other Hon. Member that they are not. If so, I withdraw the suggestion. Just the same, they have import, as I said a moment ago. At least I have their attention.
December 14, 1983

I will try to put into context what they did finally with my argument about "watch out" for manipulation and cynicism from the Official Opposition, selective readings of the public comments I made to serve their own purposes.
As I was saying before I was interrupted a moment ago, what is very important in this critical time in Canada when the press, politics, the major elements, the major public institutions of our democracy are held in so little credibility, is that we all do a better job of just working at what we honestly believe in and do a little less well at manipulating polls, crowds and headlines. That is really the point I wanted to make.
If I may speak now on multiculturalism, the major thrust of something I wanted to address in the few moments I have left, for too long multiculturalism in the minds of many Canadians, in public perception, has been a policy that applies to newcomers, to others, to non-Anglophones, non-Francophones, Anglo-Celts and French-Canadians. Now it has become the mainstream policy. Its inclusion in the Constitution, which is something for which I commend the Government, has helped make that happen.
I want to issue a warning, if I can as somebody who served longer as Minister of Multiculturalism than anyone else in this House. If it is a policy to bring people together, if it is a policy to fight for equity, if it is a policy to build self-esteem, if it is a policy in a country as diverse as our own, as Canadians we have to respect each other and we have to build those bridges and draw together and fight for those newly come or here for many years who are not well treated versus others, then it is a wonderful opportunity as a society in public policy to help bring about the national unity which we will always be striving for to bring this very large and very diverse country together.
Let me caution that should it be a policy to divide, to build blocs, to identify simply by ethnicity and country of origin, to encourage old country debates in the public sphere, some of them quite legitimate, it will be detrimental. It will help divide our nation and it will hurt rather than help us.
I am very proud that during the time that I served as Minister of Multiculturalism, we saw a great many developments which I believe, with the support of my caucus colleagues and Cabinet, set us on the road to making it a societal concept. It has also set us on the road, at last, to putting a social face on it. The new programs for immigrant women are too often ignored. We hear a lot of talk and there is a lot of pressure to give women their equal due in Canadian society, yet too often elements of that part of society which is made up of women have been left behind.
The fight against racism in a country that is evolving very rapidly in our immigrant numbers and sources, the ability I believe to give due credit to all sides of the House for this House to establish a special parliamentary committee to look at the problem of racism in Canada and to look, most important, not at the grievances of individuals but to look at the institutional barriers, look at the police forces, look at the teachers' groups in various of our communities, look at the major pieces of society, the business sector, the Chamber of Commerce, and say: "Do they in their establishment reflect a
The Address-Mr. Fleming
cross-section of the society we are, and if they don't why don't they?" I give credit to the Government for being supportive and allowing that to take place and to Members on all sides for being supportive in giving unanimous consent to have it take place.
Of course, as I mentioned earlier, Clause 27 is surely a very important development. I wanted to put on the record a few words about a cause that is close to my heart. If it is a tag-on, a pawn to organize ethnic leaders, an afterthought for a third force, multiculturalism would be disastrous. If it is a societal policy, recognizing all Canadians, bringing us together and teaching us to respect whatever our numbers, wherever we settle, whatever our roots, then it is a very positive policy and deserves strong support from all sides of this House.
In the few minutes remaining, I would simply like to touch on the issue of a free press. A handful, because that is all there is left, of daily newspaper publishers in this country raised a terrible uproar, with the support of the Official Opposition, over an effort by this Government to try to put into context the ownership of daily newspapers in this country. Almost every Canadian city that had daily newspapers only has one now. Only two or three Canadian cities now have competing daily newspapers.
There is no doubt in my mind or in the mind of anybody who has studied the media in Canada that the agenda of the media is set by the daily press. At this time there are two companies, Southam and Thomson, who together in English-language circulation control almost two-thirds of Canadian daily newspapers. It seems to me that that is an unhealthy level. At the very least, we should encourage others to build up in competition.
The simple fact that a young reporter does not go out working for one daily newspaper in a Canadian city, competing with a young reporter working for another daily newspaper, militates against the kind of accuracy, the kind of extra story, the added element that will give Canadians true content in news reporting across this country. When you, with all the benevolence in the world for those two companies, give them the benefit of any doubt, when you have only two operating with so much, the little bits that are left are in jeopardy in that they are unable to have the kind of excellence necessary to compete.
When you are the only newspaper in town, will you spend as much money on your editorial content? Will you dig as hard to dig out the story, the dirt, the scandal, the misbehaviour by someone? Indeed, a democracy operates on a competitive free press, and in the daily newspaper industry there is far too much concentration. I hope, as difficult as it is to take on that handful of publishers who control so much, that this Government will be prepared to state that it will not allow further concentration of ownership in that industry.
In the few minutes left, the only other point I want to make is that when there is only one daily newspaper in town, when the print has so much power, there should be a vehicle of complaint short of the courts or the benevolence of the editor

December 14, 1983
The Address-Mr. La Salle
of that newspaper when a group or an individual feel they have not been treated fairly by that powerful part of democracy.
I am delighted that now we have voluntary press councils across this country, with the exception of Saskatchewan, and I hear it is happening there soon. It was the threat of a National Advisory Council on Newspapers which made that happen over the last 15 or 18 months.
Let me put on the record that I still believe there is a reason for concern if those councils are paid for by the publishers and if the primary and initial appointments are made by the publishers. Then there is a vested interest, at least an appeared conflict of interest with all the benevolence in the world of the members of those councils. Canadians have the right to a free press. It is essential to a healthy democracy, especially when there are so many techniques, so many means, such advance technology today to try to play with the public's mind.
I think I will end on that point, and I welcome any questions.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to make a few comments on this distinguished document, referred to as the Speech from the Throne. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have heard quite a few Speeches from the Throne in the last fifteen years, and with the veteran Members of this House, I must say it is always an impressive series of good intentions, but this year, the Government, in the light of the utter fiasco it has perpetrated, has tried to please everyone with good intentions, before it calls an election. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member who just spoke referred to manipulation. Today is December 14, and four years ago on this very day, I think Canadians will remember they witnessed an extraordinary exercise in manipulation when the Government promised not to increase the price of gas by our proposed eighteen cents, and the result is history. If that is not manipulation, I don't think our friends on the opposite side should accuse the Progressive Conservative Party of manipulating, because Canadians have witnessed a lot of manipulation in various areas over the last fifteen years.
Mr. Speaker, like many Canadians, the people in my riding are worried. Farmers are worried and the unemployed are worried too. Young people are worried, and they are aware of the Government's poor management and administration, confirmed once again yesterday by the Auditor General's Report, where it is recognized that for I don't know how many consecutive years, the Government has been unable to control its expenditures and has failed to make adequate efforts to establish proper mechanisms. But all this matters very little to the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau)
because he feels that after all, there have been a few improvements under his administration, and that we should ignore the strict recommendations and accusations being made by the Auditor General.
Mr. Speaker, we are aware of our responsibilities and that we must demand that this Government provide proper administration of the public purse and see to it that public monies are wisely spent, something it has failed or has yet to understand.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, reading the Speech from the Throne from beginning to end is not going to make us more inclined to trust this Government, considering the exercise we have seen during the last fifteen years which 1 witnessed first hand. It is a fact that in the Speech from the Throne, the vast majority of its proposals and the funds that are or will be appropriated, were already announced in the April Budget, and the Government has been making undertakings on that basis for a number of months already. There is the figure of $ 1 billion which may impress Canada's youth, and speaking of manipulation, perhaps it would be useful to look at this attempt by the Government to manipulate Canadian youth, when it refers to new funding of SI billion, which was quickly deflated by the Minister responsible, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts). Actually, only 25 per cent of the SI billion was new money and if we figure how many jobs paying S200 per week for a period of twenty weeks would be available, $250 million would provide jobs for not more than 10 per cent of the 545,000 people looking for employment in Canada. Their problems have not been solved, far from it.
Now, the Government had the clever idea of creating or inventing a Ministry of Youth. Of course we have nothing against anyone being specifically responsible for job creation for young people. We are all for it. But, Mr. Speaker, if a Ministry of Youth were enough to solve the problem of unemployment among our young people who are almost desperate, we should attack the Government for not having acted sooner. It is a fact that this new Ministry of Youth will be taking over programs from various Departments and will therefore have more or less the same programs plus $250 million for the coming year. Mr. Speaker, you will agree that this is not responding to the expectations of our young people. If the Government really wants to step up its activity in job creation for young people, it can count on our support and on a very positive contribution on our part. However, it should not give our young people the impression, or try to give that impression in a forthcoming election, that this new mechanism that is to be called the Ministry of Youth will solve all their problems. That is not quite where the answer to the problem lies.
Mr. Speaker, I have also been a regular listener to speeches by party leaders, and I heard the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada talk about challenge. Last night on television, they
December 14, 1983

were talking about challenge and last night in Toronto, the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada was stressing the importance of facing challenges, and he asked Canadians to put their trust in him for the future. I imagine a few Liberals were disappointed, but as far as this side is concerned, Mr. Speaker, if the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada wants to talk about the future, he ought to mention both his accomplishments and the problems for which he has been responsible as Prime Minister of Canada during the last twenty years, since he mentioned accomplishments in the debate on the Throne Speech and again last night in Toronto.
Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada spoke to the House about the patriation of the Constitution, and the fact that he succeeded in patriating the Constitution to Canada. He was, of course, very proud of the latest legislation on the Crow. The Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada can tell the House about his consultations with the Provinces. Still, the Prime Minister and our friends opposite ought to remember and realize that Canadians as well will remember that the first challenge proposed by the Prime Minister 15 years ago- I, for one, remember-had to do with a just society which was to meet the aspirations of all Canadians in every walk of life throughout the country.
Several years ago, as I recall, the Prime Minister of Canada was also promoting this dialogue and this cooperation as being essential to the viability of a renewed federalism, the fad words of 15 years already. History will record that the Prime Minister, through almost daily confrontation, succeeded in tearing his own country apart with respect to federal-provincial relations. And then, everybody knows that this Government has often engaged in direct competition with the private sector, vital as it is if we are to have a healthy economic recovery. The Government now acknowledges that it has failed miserably to appreciate the cooperation it could have had from the private sector and, in a complete about-turn, after being so arrogant, it dispatches the Minister of Finance to woo and beg the private sector to join in this economic recovery which, according to the Minister of Finance, is well under way. However, we are not so sure about that.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is mistaken if he really believes that the Canadian people will continue to follow him and have confidence in him, he who accuses the Progressive Conservative Party of seeking to drag the country back to the 14th century. The way things are going now, what with the national debt which has gone from $11 billion to $150 billion in 15 years, and the number of unemployed which has soared from 300,000 to 2 million, again in 15 years, I am not at all convinced that this Government will carry us into the 20th century. The Prime Minister may be worried about the possibility of a Conservative Government dragging the country back to the 14th century, but I am afraid that Canadians will never make it to the 20th century if they continue to be administered as they are today.
The Address-Mr. La Salle
When the Prime Minister of Canada points the finger at the Progressive Conservative Party for being against everything, he forgets something. He forgets to say that most Canadians are against his own Government. That is not wishful thinking on the part of the Progressive Conservative Party, the figures are there and, according to the latest polls, the trend is unmistakable. When the Prime Minister claims that we were against the Constitution, he is shamelessly lying to the people, and I will explain just what I mean. We have never been against the principle of patriating the Constitution, but we did speak strongly against the way the Government wanted to proceed, and today we are pleased that we were able to force the Government to hold public hearings, particularly since the Prime Minister was against that. It was imperative to patriate the Constitution, but in his own way. In principle, therefore, we were not against bringing back the Constitution. Among other things, we would have hoped that constructive discussions would have led the ten provinces to agree on patriation. We certainly cannot be held responsible for the fact that one province was left out, a province I know well because it was Quebec. It was not party to the patriation agreement and it did not support the Government because of the way it sought to reach a consensus.
The Prime Minister has taken the Progressive Conservative Party to task for being against the metric system, whereas in fact we wanted and fought for freedom for Canadians to use either the metric or the imperial system. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, we were in favour of freedom of expression, but against compulsory implementation of the metric system. Scornful remarks will be heard as well about the position of the Progressive Conservative Party on health insurance. Mr. Speaker, I am saying-and so will my colleagues-that we are all in favour of Canadians getting the best health care in this country, and we strongly support every improvement in that field. Any Member of the House who would claim that we are against improved health care and against health insurance for Canadians would be very dishonest. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, particularly when we keep in mind the current situation as well as the concern, insecurity and despair expressed by Canadians from coast to coast! In Quebec and throughout all of Canada, people are tremendously concerned with the way we have been governed. And rightly so. Of course, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will try to side-track the discussion, to bring in the issue of world peace. Let me tell you right now and then that I am profoundly in favour of peace. You are also. Everyone is. We are all for motherhood. What chances does the Prime Minister have of saving Canada from a nuclear war? They are not better than mine in my view. Not better than those of any Hon. Member in this House. Of course, we will welcome and support any peace initiative. There is no question about that. But let not the Prime Minister try and make Canadians believe he is the only one capable of preventing a nuclear war. He might be tempted to do so. I know the Prime Minister well. He will probably try to get Canadians to

December 14, 1983
The Address-Mr. La Salle
discuss that issue he feels is so immensely important. Of course it is important, but there are domestic problems in Canada. The fact is that the Prime Minister has responsibilities in Canada. He and his Ministers are accountable to the Canadian people. That is what we want to discuss over the next few months anyway, and without ignoring the importance of world peace. They should not expect us to forget their mismanagement. They can make Canadians forget the sufferings they have witnessed because of their failures and their lack of adequate policies that could have helped us weather the recession with less pain.
I have listened carefully to our Leader's speech. The Prime Minister and his group will go on repeating that the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party was unable to announce proposals, programs. But, I read his speech carefully, and I read it again before speaking this afternoon, because I wanted to be sure whether the Prime Minister had told the truth to the Canadian people. But I am not as yet convinced that the Prime Minister has told Canadians the whole truth. When the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, our Party, in a responsible way, commits himself to provide adequate funding for research and development in order to create jobs, does that not indicate a well-defined orientation, when the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party requires that this Government finally acknowledge the importance of more research? Nothing can be more positive in my view than for the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party to recognize this lack of adequate productivity, the extent of such inadequate productivity in the face of foreign competition, with a commitment that his Party's and his Government's policies will be aimed at promoting greater productivity in Canadian industry. Is that not something clear and specific, even though the Prime Minister finds it hard to understand it?
We are privileged with having a Party Leader who knows about business, who is aware of the role of industry and of the industrial potential of Canada on the world scene, and is experienced in labour relations, and when the Prime Minister in the Throne Speech states the Government's intention to meet around the same table with labour and management. But I have heard of that intention, of that proposal ten times already, Mr. Speaker. However this Government once again has failed to meet with those various representatives to pursue the common goal of job creation, to put the unemployed back on the labour market and also to give a chance to our young people who have lost all hope of ever assuming their rightful place on the labour market.
It is rubbish, Mr. Speaker, all the good intentions we read about in the Throne Speech when after 15 and 20 years they could not, or did not deem fit to sit down with those groups that are so essential to the defining of medium- and long-term policies. Let us make good use of the private sector, Mr. Speaker, rather than have the Government compete with it, let
us make good use of the private sector, let us define long-term economic orientations that will restore the Canadian business climate and give people the incentives needed to invest rather than have the Government supplant the private sector, as has so often occurred over these last few years. Such is the kind of leadership the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party has advocated in his speech and on every Canadian forum. He missed no opportunity to emphasize the role of the private sector in job creation. The economic recovery is also a matter of confidence, Mr. Speaker and the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) who so seriously hampered the oil industry could surely not lay claim to the cooperation and trust of the private and business sectors today. Mr. Speaker, how could those politicians still believe that they can regain public confidence when public polls tell us they have been overwhelmingly rejected?
Mr. Speaker, are we not entitled to demand a popular verdict after such a failure, when so many people want an opportunity to make a judgment based on this government's record and not on promises made by the Prime Minister of Canada? That is why, Mr. Speaker, in a democratic system, we should demand that an election be called.
Our leader as well as our party are aware of the stability and security now needed by farmers, new home buyers and homeowners generally. What are the policies now implemented to give that sense of security in the agricultural and housing sectors? Of course, a commitment has been made in the Speech from the Throne. We will learn more about it later on. But God knows what the housing sector has gone through during the past three, four or five years, due to the lack of proper policies, except for a last minute and costly makeshift policy. For example, no steps had been taken to forestall the worst. In the farming sector, the situation is similar. I know that in my own province of Quebec, some areas are experiencing unusual problems this winter as a result of weather conditions last summer. There is no assurance that those farmers will be helped. How many of my colleagues have asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to help them get through a period of crushing interest rates. It is a fact that funds made available to the Farm Credit Corporation have been increased, which does not mean that the farming community's burden has been lightened.
Mr. Speaker, you are aware of the need to ensure the survival of the farming community and to implement a housing policy, in winter, in Canada, people require good housing. As far as farm policies are concerned, we must ensure that our people eat three meals a day. And because of the difficult times we are experiencing now, Mr. Speaker, in the absence of a policy to protect them from huge interest rates, farmers could not be persuaded to invest, or young Canadian men and women to become homeowners. There is no adequate policy to protect these people and their commitments. Long term policies of this type are absolutely essential to convince individual
December 14, 1983

Canadians, men and women, that the several thousand dollars they will invest will be secure.
I regret that my time has expired. There are still a great many things I should like to say. You certainly understand why, like most Canadians, 1 could no longer trust this Government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate, rising after my Hon. friend from Joliette who has clearly demonstrated the void in the Progressive Conservative Party platform. It is quite an achievement to speak for 20 minutes without saying anything. I might exaggerate somewhat, Mr. Speaker, as I was a little late-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, somewhat!

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Just the same, it is an ability which alas! we on this side do not have. When the Hon. Member speaks the way he just did, he seems to be following the example of his leader. I was in the House when the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party (Mr. Mulroney) made his speech, a very impressing and amusing one at that, but which contained nothing. But it was a very amusing speech just the same. [English]
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that I thought the Leader of the Conservative Party was most amusing in the House when he accused the Government of stealing Tory ideas for the Throne Speech. I must say that this did not receive a lot of laughter at that time, but upon reflection, Mr. Speaker, surely that was the most amusing part of the speech. We all know that we could not even be accused of petty theft in that regard. It does not take a lawyer to know that you cannot steal that which does not exist. The only accusation I suppose he could levy against us had we used any Tory ideas, which as I mentioned is impossible, would be surely that of bad judgment. I heard the other day, Mr. Speaker, a propos of that, that the press has a way of knowing when they receive a brown envelope from the Tory Research Bureau. Do you know how they know that? The envelope is empty.
It is quite remarkable that we have on the other side of the House a political Party which promotes itself as the Party of the 1980s, and yet has not produced one single policy resolution since the 1970s. It is a bit unfair to accuse the Leader of the Opposition, because at least during the leadership contest he produced a thin book entitled Where I Stand and, of course, we know that all Hon. Members on that side of the House have taken five or ten minutes to read the book to learn where they think they stand. As I mentioned the other day, I am told
The Address-Mr. Johnston
that that book, if it is reprinted, will likely bear the title "Where I Stood".
We also know that the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) are very concerned that in fact the Leader might produce some policies because they, as wise men of the Party, have taken the position that one should not stand at all. "Elect us", they say, "then we will tell you where we stand".
Our Party, of course, Mr. Speaker, takes a completely different tack, and it seems to me that that is clear from the Throne Speech itself. This afternoon, in the brief time available to me, I would like to deal with a few of the economic aspects of the Throne Speech, in the context of today's economy, the economy which Canada faces as a member of the western industrialized world in 1983. Is the Party opposite prepared to stand some good news, because there is some good news. I know that those Hon. Members prefer to see a glass as half empty rather than half full, but in fact, it is more than half full.
I was interested in noting yesterday the comments of my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). He in fact produced some of the good news which I am about to unveil to Hon. Members in this House. I have in my hand, Mr. Speaker, the very prestigious international magazine Euromoney, which is published in the United Kingdom. Hon. Members on the opposite side of the House will know that it is perhaps the most prestigious magazine of its kind. There is an interesting article in the October edition entitled "The Resurgence of the Industrial Economies". One finds that of the 10 most improved economies in 1983-10 out of 93-Canada is number one. Canada is number one out of 93 countries in the world in terms of improved performance in 1983. Not many Canadians know that, and I know my friends on that side of the House- and I include my friends in the New Democratic Party- would prefer that Canadians not know that. However, that happens to be a fact. I would like simply to read one brief passage:
But since the beginning of this year the performance of the main industrialized countries has been remarkable. Canada's GDP has swung from a decline of nearly 5 per cent last year to a 7.2 per cent annualized growth rate for the second quarter of this year, though the fourth quarter figure will probably be lower. Canada's recovery has been greatly influenced by improving conditions in the United States, with increases in export demand outstripping domestic demand increases.
That statement makes us realize what all Canadians have, I believe, painfully learned, and as the Minister of Finance himself stated during question period today, that Canada, being a trading nation, is very much dependent upon what happens in the rest of the world and particularly in the United States.
I am heartened by some of the projections for the United States. It was brought to my attention earlier today that a very prominent economic forecaster, Charles B. Reeder of the DuPont Corporation in the United States, is really quite bullish in what he sees happening south of the border. He tells us that in 1984 total employment should rise by over three million to an all-time peak, and unemployment should decline

December 14, 1983
The Address-Mr. Johnston
another million during 1984; that industrial production will continue rising, registering an annual gain of between 8 per cent and 10 per cent. Corporate profits should increase more than 30 per cent; the rate of inflation should remain low with the CPI rising 4 per cent to 5 per cent over 1983; interest rates should decline one to three percentage points, and the federal deficit should shrink by at least $30 billion from 1983's record of $195 billion. Of course, Mr. Speaker, that is in the United States, but we have to keep a weather eye on the United States to know where the Canadian economy is going, and I suggest that we are going to do very well indeed, moving into 1984.
These forecasts are indeed exciting. I might also say that the economic initiatives of this Government-not only those outlined in the Throne Speech, but the initiatives and the Budget of last April, the Special Recovery Capital Projects Program, and so on, have been very supportive in contributing to and reinforcing the momentum of this economic performance of which we are all proud.

Mr. Speaker, I would now like to mention some aspects of the Throne Speech which are intented to buttress this economic recovery. First, a few themes were mentioned in the Throne Speech, and I would like to read two of them:
To attain these goals, a comprehensive program will be presented:
-I especially want to refer to these two objectives:
-to encourage economic growth so that more Canadians can own a home, learn
a trade, expand a business, participate in the ownership of our resources and
gain a fair share of the abundant benefits this country can provide;
-to develop new partnerships among business, labour, government and other
groups so that together we will build a better future;
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to continue not only to describe certain goals, but also to point out some of the initiatives which will be taken to promote these objectives. Once again, 1 refer to the Throne Speech, especially with regard to the challenge of creating jobs, and I quote:
Using re-allocated and new resources, a $1 billion Youth Opportunity Fund will assist young Canadians in acquiring new skills and in finding jobs in the private, voluntary and public sectors. In particular, substantial resources from this Fund will be allotted to a career access program which encourages the private sector to provide work and training to those entering the workforce for the first time.
I would now like to go on to something else, but before I do so, I want to give a concrete example, and I quote once more:
To ensure a strong national economy capable of providing jobs and meeting the needs of all Canadians, wherever they may live, federal programs and funding have already been re-organized in a new Industrial and Regional Development Program. It will support recovery through concrete initiatives, taking maximum advantage of the strengths and attributes of every region.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, thanks to the efforts of our colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley), under the same program, namely IRDP, Bell Helicopter will build a plant in Quebec. This will mean a permanent industry in Quebec and 2,700 permanent jobs, all in the field of high technology, which is so important for Canada.
However, Mr. Speaker, my colleague did not stop there. He went even further, and I would like to mention the Pratt and
Whitney project, which will make it possible to create 6,000 jobs in the Montreal area, in addition to the trickle down effect it will have in other regions of Canada and its impact on our exports.
He has not stopped with that program referred to in the Throne Speech. Just yesterday, as Members of this House know, the Minister advised us that a memorandum of understanding had been entered into with a West German company, MBB, for the fabrication of more helicopters, another type, in Fort Erie.

speechtext: That is right, in my riding, an area of high unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Again that will create 760 jobs, of which 160 will be at Pratt & Whitney. These are concrete examples of that statement in the Throne Speech. These are real, longterm, permanent jobs in a high technology area that will be of immense benefit to Canada, not only for domestic purposes but also for exports.
With that, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to pass very rapidly to another exciting initiative, the new era of federal-provincial planning and consultation which has been launched, and which comes directly under my responsibility as the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development. The Government will be entering into Economic and Regional Development Agreements with all the provinces in due course, as has already been done with the Province of Manitoba. Negotiations are well under way in a number of other provinces.
What is significant about these agreements, Mr. Speaker, is that they herald a new era of federal-provincial planning on economic development. There is only one economy in this country, only one in each province, and it is this kind of agreement which will enable a maximum amount of synergism to take place between programs at the provincial level and those at the federal level. This is done of course within the framework, as 1 have often described in this House and before committee, of the role of the Federal Economic Development Co-ordinators and the role of the Economic Development perspectives in each province, and ultimately the Economic Regional Development Agreements and subsidiary agreements which will be entered into pursuant to those agreements. In fact, the whole economic development envelope of this Government is regionally sensitive and is becoming, I believe, a mainstay of the future economic development potential of this country to maximize the impact of dollars spent provincially and federally. As I mentioned, the first of the umbrella agreements was recently entered into with the Province of Manitoba.
There is of course much more in the Throne Speech with respect to economic development. The accent is placed on trade, which of course is fundamental to the health and well-being of this country and the creation of jobs. It states
December 14, 1983

there will be an aggressive trade drive, as there already has been. The current Minister and his predecessor have been particularly active, but there will be an extension of PEMD. There is a proposal for the duty-free export zones, and of course the pursuit of world product mandates. There is the very important commitment to continue to make Canadian industry competitive on a world class basis. What better and concrete evidence of that could we have than the R and D proposals discussed yesterday by the Minister of Finance and which are currently before the House with respect to amendments to the Income Tax Act? These proposals, put forth in the April Budget, were the subject of representations by the private sector. The Minister has responded with a new, imaginative system to direct equity funds into some of these young, aggressive and growing high technology companies. 1 say that this is the kind of initiative which is going to create jobs and wealth for Canada. It clearly keeps with the economic development thrust in the Throne Speech.
I cannot let pass the reference to NSERC, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council touched on in the Throne Speech debate where additional funding will be provided.
One thing I have come to realize very quickly, Mr. Speaker, in the discharge of my responsibilities in government, is that the greatest resource this country has is not oceans, forests, agriculture, or energy-it is the people. In this period when we move into what is called the information society, namely the application of knowhow, we need skilled and highly qualified manpower more than we have ever needed in the past. That will enable us to apply these new emerging technologies to tradtional sectors to ensure they remain competitive on world markets. That requires a quality of life environment to train and keep those people in Canada. For that purpose the Throne Speech is also significant as there is a stepping out in the speech to move more and more toward better consultation between business, labour and government. This, of course, is fundamental to the alliance I referred to a moment ago in my opening remarks as one of the themes of this Throne Speech. That alliance is essential to make this country more productive than it has even been in the past.
Time does not permit me to go over the inventory of economic development initiatives found in this speech, Mr. Speaker, but before I close 1 cannot help but comment on certain criticisms made by others. For example, I refer to some comments offered by John Bulloch of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. I must say I have a great deal of time usually for the comments of Mr. Bulloch, and I attribute some of his comments to the fact that he may not have really had time to digest the speech as he otherwise might have wished to do. I see, for example, that he said they were looking for promises on long overdue competition and bankruptcy bills. Well, if one looks at the Throne Speech, one will find the following statement:
Following extensive and continuing consultations with the private sector and the provinces, the Government will introduce a new competition policy to bring market forces to bear in the continuing fight against inflation.
The Address-Mr. Johnston
It goes on to say what that legislation is going to do. Again I can say the same with respect to comments made by the President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. He said:
What we needed was a vigorous message giving us a sense of purpose and vision concentrating on the need to improve our competitiveness, stimulate investment and reduce the government deficit.
The Throne Speech does all of those, Mr. Speaker. When we speak of vision-[DOT]

-Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that this speech shows real vision. It mentions world peace, economic growth, and the new partnership of which I have already spoken, which will protect and enrich our social programs of which we are so proud, and reinforce our Canadian identity. In my opinion, this represents the vision of Canada for the 80s.

Mr. Speaker, it is easily understood on this side that the Government would not wish to improve its election affections that Canadians presently have for it by speaking about its past record. It will have to rely on forecasts or perhaps on its usual luck for the Opposition to make some pronouncements, which could then be attacked and used by the Government in the next election.
I have a question for the Minister which relates to the Speech from the Throne and to his particular interest, to which he has not made reference today, for the need to improve our industry's productivity in order for it to compete once again more effectively in world markets. That serious matter is raised in the Throne Speech and a solution is offered. That solution is a system of awards for companies and workers who would show significant productivity gains.
The workers and companies with whom I have been associated in my business career would prefer to have the rewards instead of awards. They would like to have rewards and have those reflected in the balance sheet or in their pay cheques. What kind of awards does the Minister have in mind? Will people get a medal which will be reminiscent of coal mines and salt mines in the Soviet Union? What is the system of awards that the Minister has in mind that will bring about this improvement in the productivity of our industry?
