subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to have an opportunity to speak for my Party on the Throne Speech. We are only a few days away from Christmas and the Throne Speech certainly presented two wishes to Canadians that I would also like to present to all Canadians, that is, the wish for peace and the wish for prosperity. I do not believe that there is anything that human beings would ask for more than to have peace and prosperity in their own lives. Today we live in a world in which peace and prosperity are not known by many people, not only those who live in actual war zones but people who live in very modern cities. There are many people there who live without peace and prosperity.
I would like to direct my remarks to certain areas where I have had some experience and knowledge. The procedure during this Throne Speech debate has been for each Member to speak in relation to his or her background and skill and make his critique of the plans the Government has put forward to bring about peace and prosperity. As we have seen, there are many critiques of what has taken place and what has been proposed.
At Christmas time those of us who still believe in Santa Claus look forward to the presents which he hands out from the big bag he carries. Interestingly enough, the only riding in Canada that was specifically mentioned in the Throne Speech was my own riding of Saskatoon East, although it was not called by that name. However, indication was made in the Throne Speech that a present is coming to Saskatoon East. It is the hydrology laboratory which is to be built at the university there. I sincerely hope that this present arrives since it has been offered to Saskatoon many times. It was one of the major gifts that my good friend and former opponent, Otto Lang, used to present once in a while although we never really received it. Of course, when poor Otto went down the road and
my Conservative friends came to power, they wiped out that present. During the last three or four years the Government has been indicating again that the present is ready to be sent. According to the Throne Speech, it is on the way. 1 hope that this time this necessary laboratory will arrive at the University of Saskatchewan. It will be very beneficial to have it there. I was speaking to the President of the University last week, Dr. Leo Kristjanson, and he indicates that its plans are ready and the tenders should be going out in January. While the Throne Speech did not really tell us something new, I hope it reaffirms that this laboratory is there to stay this time.
The introduction of the Throne Speech basically revolved around the theme of peace. In this respect I certainly want to commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for what he has been doing during recent weeks and days in attempting to find some space between President Reagan and Chairman Andropov. I believe the world has arrived at a point of international tension where we could easily be triggered into a nuclear confrontation which nobody wants. It does not matter whether it is the Prime Minister of Canada, a Member of the House or anyone else, if someone can find some space to reduce international tension I feel they should be told to continue.
At the same time, I would like to offer my best wishes to the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) who has been given the responsibility of disarmament on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party. Several weeks ago the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead attended a conference in New York in which I also participated. It was a conference at the United Nations of Parliamentarians for World Order. I was very pleased to see the Right Hon. Member present at this conference. He was taking part with this group of parliamentarians, some 900 from around the world, who have dedicated themselves to using their parliamentary responsibilities toward disarmament of the world and the development of people. The Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead has been asked by his Leader to represent his Party in the quest to solve this problem of disarmament, and I want to offer him my sincerest best wishes, as I have already offered to him privately, in helping to find success in this endeavour.
I believe it is important to recognize that the Conservative caucus, perhaps through the efforts of their Leader, has been able to show that with respect to external affairs there will perhaps be a blend. To many people, my good friend, the hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) who has been given the position of external affairs critic, seems to be pretty far down the road to the right. I was talking to him the other day in the airport, as we and many others were waiting for our planes in the rain, and he told me that many of his right wing friends are now beginning to call him "Sine, the Pink". I doubt that that name is true, but this is what he told me. His friends are calling him "Sine, the Pink" because he is not really showing that right wing tenacity which he had shown during the time he had been on the External Affairs Committee.
December 14, 1983

At this time I would like to point out both to the Prime Minister and to the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead that I believe that, unless they decide that testing the Cruise missile in Canada takes away their credibility as peace finders, they will not find an easy road to fulfilling their responsibilities. There is still time for the Government to stop the testing of the Cruise missile in Canada. The Prime Minister and the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead could do that, and both of them can ask for that, but we must remember that when there was a vote in this House several months ago on the testing of the Cruise missile it was only the New Democrats, four Members of the Progressive Conservative Party and one Liberal who voted against that. That is something we have to keep in mind when we push ahead on this question of disarmament and getting away from an atomic confrontation.
It is obvious, and many people are aware of the fact, that one of the major problems facing the world is the whole question of armaments sales. I could go into this subject at great length. It is going to be something like $700 billion this year. We also must remember that since the end of the Second World War something like 140 wars have been fought and 30 million people killed. What is happening here and what the Throne Speech is telling us is that the Government is seriously making attempts to find a way to bring about mutual disarmament, and it certainly has my total support.
However, when we get to the question of total disarmament and how it affects Canadians, it is important to remember four little words, which are used very freely and easily and which have a great deal to do with the major problem. These four little words are nothing more than north-south and east-west. That section of the world commonly called the south is where most of the people live and is the area where there is massive poverty and misery. The developing countries in that part of the world have gone through a terrible past two years. Major economies like Brazil have collapsed. Mexico and other countries, and even the biggest countries in the south, have gone through just terrible economic situations and their futures look very difficult.
Interestingly enough to my mind, this tension which is happening now between those who have and those who do not have is creating a tension that could bring about, as Cardinal Carter, as reported in The Globe and Mail this week, said, a violent global revolution. When we talk about east-west being the problem, I think many times it is just covering over that the real problem is. Again on the question of north-south I would say that in the discussions which the Prime Minister has had over the past years in which he has demonstrated great skills, I feel that in the last two or three years he seems to have abandoned the project. After the meetings in Cancun, which he chaired, the question of north-south has just about disappeared, certainly from this House. Yet I believe there is a great unity between the north-south and the east-west, and a way must be found to answer those questions.
When I was studying social philosophy and economics at the University of Notre Dame several years ago, there was a
The Address-Mr. Ogle
monseigneur who had a saying that when you came to a difficult social problem, the most important thing was to be able to live the long haul. It simply meant that no matter how difficult the problem was, the person or persons who were involved in it were ready to go the distance. In the difficult questions of east-west and north-south that we are facing today I would say we have to go the distance.
The Throne Speech speaks about technological changes that are coming. I agree we must all face the changes that nobody in this House has quite imagined are going to take place. That kind of thing seems to be a long way away from the city where I live, the City of Saskatoon. Saskatoon, basically, is a small prairie city with a rural economy that gets its income from agriculture primarily but also from potash mines that are close to the city, close enough for people to live in the city and work in the mines.
During this past month there has been a situation in which technological change has brought about the laying off of 40 workers at the Imperial Optical Company Ltd. This company produces lenses for eye glasses. About 40 people were working there. They will not be there any more because they are being laid off. I think basically the reason is that technological change has made it possible to make eye glasses somewhere else faster than they can in Saskatoon.
I was very thankful that the President of the Company, Mr. Peter Herman in Toronto, replied to a letter I sent to him asking about this particular change. I was kind of shocked at the coldness with which he talks about the workers and the fact that-well, it is just too bad. In part, his letter reads:
We are confident that those employees who unfortunately had to be terminated will be well advised and hopefully compensated by their union-the United Automobile Workers-and we feel that we have behaved in the only way left open to us.
This was to get rid of their jobs, and get the automobile union to look after the workers, to look after them for the rest of their lives. That seems to be the intent.
It is interesting, and I thanked him for his openness. The President also sent me a copy of a letter that he had distributed among people who buy materials from Imperial Optical in Saskatoon. It is the first time that I find in a letter the reason for busting up a union is the six and five policy. I think that is what he is saying is the reason for terminating their service. The letter reads in part:
As you will have been aware, I am sure, the Company has been undergoing a series of negotiations with its unionized employees regarding the way in which we have been operating in the Saskatoon area. We have offered a fair and reasonable contract based on federal guidelines-
The guidelines to which he is referring, I believe, would probably be the six and five. The paragraph continues:
-and which has been accepted in all other similar operations throughout the country.
As we have said during the debate last year on the Government's policy of six and five, it seems that the six and five only affects those who are workers. I suspect the optical company- I do not have a detailed report of its holdings or what its profits were this year-has had a very good year.

December 14, 1983
The Address-Mr. Ogle
I would like to say a few words on the question of the Canadian economy, which is one of multi-faceted values. I would bring to the attention of the House again the fact that this year again the Canadian Catholic Bishops felt it was important that this subject be addressed from a moral point of view. Just a year ago in the first week of January, 1983, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops presented to the people of Canada an ethical reflection on the economic crisis. In their document they clearly pointed out some of the moral values that have to be taken into account when and during the time of an economic crisis such as ours, namely the priority of human beings over profit, in other words, the priority of the value of the human being over the making of money. In Canada there are people who are not living in prosperity and not living in peace and we have to remember that the Government has not basically addressed the problem of the unemployed. What happens to those young people? What happens to those middle-aged people who have lost their jobs and cannot get them back? What happens to those who feel that their lives have finally become useless lives because they do not have valuable employment.
Following the moral intervention which the Catholic Bishops of Canada directed to the Government last January, Cardinal Carter of Toronto indicated that he was not quite sure whether or not that was the proper approach, but wisely, I believe, set up his own commission in Toronto to study the question of the economic situation of the people of Toronto and how that is affecting the moral and family life of people in that great city.
Just this week a report has been given to the Cardinal. The quote I gave just earlier from The Globe and Mail was basically an interview he gave after the report had been given to him. It is called "Canada's Unemployed-the Crisis of Our Time". It had the input of groups of people from the Toronto area, basically, but certainly it is representative of people all over Canada.
It contained one point which I felt was very well taken because of my interest in international life and how it ties into national life. In the Bishops' statement last January, they did not bring into focus clearly enough the fact that Canada belongs to the international community and that to try to solve Canadian economic problems without looking at the international community, Third World countries or other places where cheap labour and mineral resources at lower prices are being offered, would not solve our problems. This is why it is intensely necessary that planners, whoever they may be, look a the world scene at the same time as they confront the local scene. Many times they will find that their local problem started some place else, such as in the Pacific Rimor South America. Unfortunately, in the Speech from the Throne the role of multinationals was not clearly spelled out. It was not taken into account. Many of the decisions affecting Canadian life are made by multinationals, not by local people.
The best example of that is that we in the House of Commons frequently hear people shouting "Schefferville." I know that should is directed to the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) because of the role he played in the closing down of the iron company's mines there. However, I know he did not have much to say about it. The company which closed down in Schefferville had its head office in Cleveland. It was because it knew it could obtain iron ore cheaper in Latin America. Also it knew that it could set up refineries and steel plants in South America where the governments could not defend themselves on questions of pollution, toxic waste, labour and such things. We shout the albatross word "Schefferville" at him, but basically he is a victim as well. He is the victim of a multinational which decided to use someone like that to handle its local business, and when it goes bad, that person looks like the one who is responsible.
In conclusion, in the report given to Cardinal Carter in Toronto this week, there were certain positive indications that reflect well upon the people of Canada. Although they are under stress at times because of lack of employment, they nevertheless have a practicality which we in the House of Commons should take seriously.
There are six points which can be drawn from that particular report. The first was that workable policies and practices need the insight and guidance of ordinary people as well as the best efforts of experts. Something which is very important is the wisdom of ordinary people. In discussing problems, many times experts say to do it one way and the ones who suffer are the ordinary people.
Second, most Canadians believe that there is a need for a social conscience in public and private dealings, but as yet there is no broad agreement on what exactly constitutes a social conscience. Put simply, how do we make a moral decision about a complicated social thing? Of course, I do not have any simple answer, but at the time of peace, the time of Christmas, I would at least point out a principle which should be taken into consideration for all times: "Do unto others as you would have them do unto you". We have to feel along with those who are in the suffering stage at the bottom, wherever it happens to be.
Third, the report pointed out that most people want and expect changes in thinking, attitudes, institutions, relations and changes of heart which the majority continue to believe come from within our present system. However, there is no great revolution yet, although the Cardinal conceded that if situations continue around the world there definitely could be.
Fourth, even those hurt by unemployment have a generosity of spirit, which I think is important. However, this patience can shift dramatically if there are not reciprocal efforts from institutions and individuals in positions to attempt change. That speaks very clearly to the House and to the Government.
Fifth, bigger handouts are not the best answer. The only acceptable and workable answer in the long run is to provide more opportunities for decent worth-while jobs, the kind which engender self-respect.
December 14, 1983

Finally, despite many obstacles, the panel was left with the impression of possibilities rather than one of despair. It is very important for us to know that at this time.
I thank the House for the opportunity of participating today. I congratulate the writer of the Throne Speech for the statement that institutes will be set up to study disarmament, something we on this side have recommended many times. I hope it is put into place quickly, put into place with effective funds and by people who have the understanding and knowledge to bring about true world disarmament.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this 14th day of December, it is a pleasure for me to take part in the debate on the Throne Speech, in order to elaborate on all the benefits and important measures this document contains. I would have liked the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) to be here in the House. Yesterday, I took the trouble to invite him to attend, because I was planning to talk about matters that are very familiar to both of us, namely, the whole issue of the North Shore, Sept-Iles, Schefferville, the Iron Ore company and job creation.
I would like to say, first of all, that I was rather disappointed to see that since the Leader of the Opposition took his seat in the House, he has yet to raise the issue of job creation in connection with the North Shore. When I was listening from the North Shore, when the Speech from the Throne was read and after the comments made by the Leader of the Opposition, I was surprised that he did not mention at least one sensible measure that directly concerns the people for whom he himself had worked. I am referring to the measure requested by all the mining companies, all the unions and all the North Shore mayors, and also by the same groups of people in the far North. I am referring to the exemption from taxation of northern benefits. Now, the first practical measure mentioned in the Throne Speech was one that directly concerned the Leader of the Opposition, and he did not even mention it.
About ten minutes ago I was talking to Mr. Lawrence McBearty, president of the metal workers union in my riding, and he told me that he really appreciated the work that had been done in that area. He was grateful to the Government for being aware of this issue, which is not only important to those working in Canada's North but also to the entire development of the North. While other Members are going to describe the Speech from the Throne as a set of useless measures, I would like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that some of these useless measures are of direct concern to the people of the North Shore, who have been fighting for those measures for two years. That needs to be said. Mr. Speaker, it is true that the
The Address-Mr. Maltais
Hon. Member for Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais) and the Leader of the Opposition have been and are still close friends, but I hasten to add that friendship is not synonymous with complacency and complicity. The Hon. Member for Manicouagan has never had to decide to lay off workers or to close a mine. In a few moments, if the Leader of the Opposition so wishes and if he gets to the House in time, he might want to comment on that during the ten minutes allowed for questions. But when the issue is job creation and he hopes to become Prime Minister of the country, I wish our Leader of the Opposition would change into a leader of propositions and tell us clearly what he will do to get people back to work.
I listened to his remarks concerning the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. He said that Canada had about half a million people out of work in 1968, but that we now have a million and a half unemployed. It is very easy to say just about anything in the House and elsewhere, because talk is cheap, but the facts are more important, and if I wanted to take a similar approach, I would say simply that, when Mr. Mulroney arrived in Sept-Iles in 1975 as company president, he had 7,500 employees. When he resigned to help his party, so it seems, or his former leader-I think the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) would remember those events- only 3,000 were left and that work force has since dwindled to 2,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue is job creation and unemployment. I never accused the Iron Ore Company president of being responsible for the iron crisis, regardless of all the Government assistance he was given. So much so that he came twice to see me here in the House of Commons to set up plans or Government programs to help the unemployed workers. As we say back home, he had an open and generous mind. Anyone who has heard the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition knows full well that such words are often the trademark of our Leader of the Opposition.
Mr. Speaker, this same Leader of the Opposition has been referring in his speeches to one chef and 74 meatheads. To keep to culinary terms I should like to mention that people in my riding call round shaped balls of iron pellets, and I will add that their meatballs have been changed into poison pellets because our voters preferred the Hon. Member for Manicouagan, who gave them direct assistance in their search for jobs and better conditions, over a company chairman who abandoned them to take care of his own career and perhaps that of the Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark). That, however, is the affair of the Members opposite. In my region, Mr. Speaker, what we felt the most was a deep feeling of loss at being abandoned by the first chairman of a multinational located in our region who was born in Baie Comeau. We had had expected more consideration, more persistence and more efforts on his part to help the workers, but instead, he quickly

went to take over the job of his former leader, to whom he had promised loyalty. We felt a deep loss when this happened. Mr. Speaker, this had to be said.
Moreover, when the Iron Ore Company announced generous initiatives to help its workers, as it indeed did, Mr. Speaker, half of them were paid by the Federal Government, the Government of Canada. In the case of other programs, the province of Quebec paid 25 per cent and the Iron Ore Company paid the rest. I must say that the Hon. Member for Manicouagan negotiated these programs with the chairman of the company.
I have here all kinds of papers from which I could quote and give dates to show that the chairman himself stated during his press conference in February before he left for the Progressive Conservative Convention in Winnipeg that if he had waited until then to give his conference, it was because he was waiting for the telegram of the Hon. Member for Manicouagan confirming the final details of the programs which would be offered to the workers.
Mr. Speaker, the Government and the Hon. Member for Manicouagan did so much in this regard that I was treated somewhat off-handedly by Department of Employment and Immigration officials because they thought that I was in too great a hurry. It seldom happens that a Government is accused of being in too great a hurry. However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention that it was on November 2 that the company chairman announced that the Schefferville plant would close on June 30 and that it was only in February that all the programs for the workers were put together. Throughout November, December, January and February, the workers were kept in complete darkness about their future. You have to come from these places to know what it means, Mr. Speaker.
This Government has been accused of not doing its job, and as I pointed out earlier, you can say just about anything in this House, but I would like to challenge the Leader of the Opposition, and I would have liked him to be here as I wanted to tell him that if the people of Sept-Iles and Schefferville in the Manicouagan riding were able to get a new start honourably and freely, it is thanks to the initiatives taken both by the Government and the company. This is important to note. I give the Leader of the Official Opposition credit for the strategy and the half truths. I find it unacceptable for the Leader of the Official Opposition to accuse this Government of inconsistency. Indeed, on March 16, 1982, the Leader of the Opposition, who was then chairman of the Iron Ore Company, attended a press conference given by the Hon. Charles Lapointe and myself concerning the assistance which would be given to the company and the workers. At that time, the chairman of Iron Ore said, and I can quote him from memory as I know by heart what he said in my region: "This is one of the best Government programs ever and it will help our company and the workers to come out of the current crisis." I would like him
to repeat it because it is easy to go from Vancouver to Halifax and say just about anything or at least only half truths, Mr. Speaker.
When I listen to my friend, the Leader of the Opposition tell the Canadian people: You know, I lived in Baie-Comeau where I used to be a truck driver. My father had two jobs in order to make ends meet. Let me tell you that in Sept-Iles and in Schefferville, there are a lot of people who would like to still be able to say "My father is a truck driver". Because there are no more trucks to drive in Sept-Iles and in Schefferville. And when I hear the Leader of the Opposition say that his father had two jobs to make ends meet, let me tell you that in my area, 30 per cent of the workers do not even have one job.
So one can raise a lot of emotionalism in this way. One can say a number of things to try and rouse the people. However, since it is said that the past is the guarantee of the future, let me quote the Leader of the Opposition, who said in Quebec City: "Watch out, Canadians". Yes, you had better watch out because the only people that were saved by the president of that company are its shareholders. Meanwhile, the Member of Parliament and his Government were trying to save the workers and the citizens. That is the difference between being president of a corporation and being a public office holder and dealing with the business of the nation. It is important not to lose sight of this distinction. I don't know what would have happened to the North Shore if the Government had not taken action. Even the Iron Ore Corporation was against the Pointe-Noire project which required investments of $46 million. Yet, this project will be the key to our economic development. We have always been happy with the various private companies that have come into our area in the past, so long as they reinvest in the area and respect the social fabric and the language of the people in Quebec. Those are the three conditions we require from the private sector for the economic development on the North Shore. But when I hear the Leader of the Opposition say that FIRA is not important, let me remind you that when the company decided to close down its operations, they did not ask the opinion of the workers. Last Saturday, I was with the steelworkers who told me: "Mr. Maltais, we now realize the importance of Government control over corporations". Because private sector people never need the Government when things are going good, they just take in the profits and the dividends. However, when the going gets bad, they are running to ministers and to Members of Parliament to get some public money, to deal with problems arising out of decisions taken in other areas, such as the decision to close down the only mine operated in Quebec by the Iron Ore Corporation. They did not close down their mines in Labrador City and in Wabush. They closed down their mine in Quebec. Who decided that, Mr. Speaker? Was it the corporate board in Cleveland or the president himself? I dont know. My friend from the other side will have the opportunity to answer that question in this House if he wants to. However, there is one
December 14, 1983

thing which is surprising, and that is this all important position of president of the corporation has never been filled since the resignation of the then president, the present Leader of the Opposition. Never!
If the Leader of the Opposition wants an election quickly, Mr. Speaker, I will challenge him to run in Manicouagan. That is where he should run. I agree there are snowstorms in winter and flies in the summer, but that is no reason why he should not run in his own area. And the only reason why I dare him to be a candidate in my riding is that the people, not the companies, are supporting me. When I say something, it is not prompted by outsiders. I share the everyday life of employed and unemployed workers, but if he can claim throughout Canada that he has helped the people on the Quebec North Shore, in Sept-Iles and in the Northern towns, he should be a candidate in the Manicouagan riding! I know that I am taking a big chance, but he would be taking a bigger one. Let him try his luck there! There are always two sides to a challenge, Mr. Speaker. I am willing to take up this challenge. I am willing to do so, because I am free to say what I want to say and because my only advisers are the workers who are supporting me.
If we were to draw a list of everything this government has done on the Quebec North Shore over the past four or five years, it would be quite long, and people are aware of it. They can see the difference between an individual who is eager to help them and one who was involved in the exploitation of the iron ore and possibly also the workers. It takes more than a well organized career plan to be able to succeed on the Quebec North Shore. It takes hard work. I issue my challenge again. And it would be quite interesting, because via satellites, the Supreme Court may now hear a case in Vancouver without having to leave Ottawa. The debate would take place on the Quebec North Shore. I would like that, because it is a region which needs to be developed. It has a bright future, but it will get nowhere if people leave it. People must stay there. I, for one, reply: Here! I have issued my challenge. In spite of the polls, I am not afraid to be a candidate opposite the Leader of the Opposition, because I have done my homework and have met my constituents one by one from the ordinary people to the unions and the presidents of companies on the same level. They are all equally important to me. But I would not go to Vancouver or Montreal to make statements which no one can verify, but on any issue which is factual and verifiable I say to the Leader of the Opposition, "Welcome!" He may be rightly proud of having been born in Baie-Comeau, but there are people who were proud of having been born in Schefferville but who may never have a chance to die there because the town is dead. Baie-Comeau on the other hand is not dead, and there is the difference. When knowing the meaning of the sense of solidarity among the people along the North Snore and in Northern communities, a solidarity which I share with the Leader of the Opposition, I would like us to have the same
The Address-Mr. Maltais
debate in our own area over the very same facts. That is important.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that my time is running out, and I hope Members opposite will allow me a few more minutes to conclude. In the Throne Speech, things are mentioned that are essential to this country's future. There is the problem of our young people. The North Shore, among other areas, is concerned with the whole issue of our young people, Mr. Speaker. For too long those people may have had to deal with too many departments. It is high time a Government truly addressed a policy for the young people. Reference is often made to resources, meaning mines, forests, rivers. But our first and foremost resource is our young people. And too often reference to them is not followed by any action. This is one of the major issues in the Throne Speech, and it should be emphasized to a greater extent by a "Leader of Proposals" opposite rather than by a Leader of the Opposition. It is ever so easy to oppose, but how more difficult to make proposals.
Another subject that deserves to be stressed in the Throne Speech is research. It is unacceptable that in a country such as Canada research is not carried out more extensively by the educational community, private industry and the various Government agencies, whether they be federal or provincial. It is most urgent that all resources be used to bring still more funds for research, because it is the minds of people that will give Canada its full dimension. I think Hon. Members on all sides of the House are in agreement to make research one of the main stays not only of our Canadian economy but of the technology that will allow us to further develop all the facets of Canada.
I know my time is running out. I would simply suggest, to conclude, that in the Throne Speech we have, for the next ten years, the keys that will turn our country onto the road to the technological, economic and social changes needed for the year 2000. We must never rely on a party that is forever reactionary, we must always have a Government bent on action and concrete proposals, Mr. Speaker.
I would like, if the Opposition will allow, to take two or three more minutes-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to rise and speak in reply to the Speech from the Throne on behalf of the riding of Wetaskiwin. During the past 11 years, 1 have always been very pleased to be the representative of the good people of the riding of Wetaskiwin who have a great spirit of enterprise and are willing to work hard in an attempt to provide security for their families and a good future for themselves within the Province of Alberta.
Most of the riding of Wetaskiwin is dependent upon an agricultural base as well as oil and gas. There is a large conventional oil and gas industry in the riding and many of the people who live there are working hard in the small business sector within the towns of the constituency or in the nearby cities of Red Deer and Edmonton.
After hearing the Speech from the Throne, we would like to believe that a new chapter will be written in history and that there will be new ideas to show the country how we will proceed in the next year. Four years have passed since the last Throne Speech, so that one really must have been a dilly because there is generally only a year to a year and a half between Throne Speeches.
There should be a plan of action within that speech so that Members of Parliament will know how their constituencies and the country will be affected. The speech should set the table for the House of Commons and the Senate by indicating what the legislative plan will be for the next year. I know that my colleagues and I will want to speak about the details which are contained within the Speech from the Throne that was read a few days ago.
During my time in the House, I have watched this Government perform for 11 years excepting for a few months. One must recognize that the way the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has operated has caused great difficulties in the nation. The Prime Minister has always believed that the manner in which he should impose his will and ideas on the country is through confrontation. Compromise has been thrown out of the window. Discussions with labour, industry, the provinces and other governments of the country only go on if those organizations are in agreement with the Prime Minister and, of course, his Cabinet has followed along in that regard. What has this done to the country?
Perhaps you could look at the situation from my perspective, Mr. Speaker, as a Member of Parliament from a western riding. You will really be able to see what has been achieved and the action that has resulted from the various Speeches from the Throne. There have been some excellent examples of that style of government in this session of Parliament. We debated the original Constitution proposal which the Prime Minister intended to force through the House over the objections of the regions. The National Energy Program wreaked devastation on the workers in my constituency. There was no consultation about the imposition of that program which had disastrous effects on the nation. Young people wanted to work in the industry in which their fathers had prospered but that work was gone. The capital escaped from the nation and the drilling rigs were closed down or moved to the United States.
OO)
Not only was there the imposition of the back-in provision but there was also the FIRA program which allowed the capital so desperately needed in that sector to leave the country. Investors were not prepared to take the risk in view of the Government's policies. There is still potential in the oil and gas industry in this country, particularly in the west, but it needs to be built up again. Nothing in the Speech from the Throne offered any assurance that this would come about. With the money it takes to drill one well in the offshore or in the north, 20 could be drilled and 20 times more people employed in the conventional oil and gas sector. The program all but destroyed the industry but it is beginning to crawl back again toward a semblance of what it once was.
In the agricultural sector, Canagrex was opposed diligently and strongly by the regions but it was forced upon them by the Government. The Crow rate had been with us for a century. Now western farmers face huge increases in the cost of production and transportation but will only receive 1970 prices for their crops. This style of government has not given anything to Canada. It offers little compromise, only confrontation. If the House of Commons stood in its way it would diminish the powers of the House. Over the years there has been more and more government by bureaucracy, not by Members of Parliament making decisions on issues that are put before them.
Opportunities to scrutinize expenditures of government are fewer than before. The Auditor General's Report has highlighted waste and the huge deficits run up year after year in the last session of this Parliament. Ministers no longer make statements in the House; they are made outside the House to the press and Members have no opportunity to question or scrutinize programs. There has been a continual downplaying of this institution because it stands in the way of the manner in which the Prime Minister and his Cabinet want to lead the country.
The Auditor General has also pointed to the growth of another subgovernment over which Members of Parliament have no control, and that is the growth of Crown corporations. Many of these inject themselves into areas where the private sector should operate. In my view, Crown corporations should only be put in place if the nation wishes to have a service and no one in the private sector is prepared to provide it. That has not been the case in recent years. Petro-Canada is an example of it.
The only success story in the House of Commons is the use of the special committees and the task forces comprised of members from all sides of the House. The reports issued by brilliant men and women, working together in compromise instead of in confrontation, have helped solve some problems in the nation. I hope the Government will use the reports that have been tabled in the past few months. Tomorrow a report on pensions will be tabled and the report on Indian self-government has just been presented. There will be others and all of them ought to be used. In the final days of this Parliament I should like to see more of this compromise rather than the
December 14, 1983

confrontation that the Prime Minister has imposed on the nation since he took over in 1968.
This attitude does not make for unity, Mr. Speaker. In my constituency, for the first time in decades I have had to face a western separatist party. Such a party is now in power in the Province of Quebec. Because certain programs have been almost shoved at the people, they have been rejected. The metric system and bilingualism are perfect examples of programs that have been imposed in the wrong manner. People will just reject them outright instead of considering how they could be adopted voluntarily.
The Government has alienated almost every sector, every region and every interest group in the country and now, in the Speech from the Throne, claims that it wants to write a new chapter which will have the answers for the country in the next few months. This must be the last chapter, Mr. Speaker. New chapters in this country with a new government should not speak of unity but should nurture it, through compromise and consultation. It should not promise economic recovery but should actively set up the foundations for it through a strong private sector and the operation of small businesses. The Government should not play with statistics but should see that the people are well represented. It should not sermonize about high ideals but should show leadership by working together to solve our problems. It has to show that anything of lasting value can be achieved only by hard work and sacrifice.
The greatest occupation as most of us know is to serve others and make sure that those people less fortunate than we can be confident that their government will work along with them instead of imposing policies without consultation. We have a highly educated population of young people who want to make the best of the abundance of resources the country offers. We are not afraid to meet the challenges of this century. We have very ably put in place the kinds of positions which we feel should be taken for this century and the kind of basic foundation which has to be built so we can move toward the 21st century.
What must that foundation be built on? One thing, as mentioned in the Throne Speech, is the youth of this nation. We have 4.5 million young Canadians between the ages of 15 and 24 in the work force. Their unemployment rate has risen from 13 per cent to over 18 per cent since 1980. These young people have gone from high school into further training because they want to build careers and have security, but they are now finding as they leave these institutions that there is nothing for them. There are no jobs. This is because of the policies I mentioned, like the National Energy Program. It is because of the lack of trust businessmen have in the taxation policies of this Government. It is because of the constant change of policy in those areas. It is because of the huge deficits and wastage of money and the imposition of central control on this nation. There is nothing there to build on. The private sector is having real difficulty in trusting this Government and as a result money is kept in the sock, in savings,
The Address-Mr. Schellenberger
instead of being put into building industry. It has affected not only small business but the larger sector.
We are not enticing people into research and development, as we were decades ago. That is lost, although we are trying to build it up again. We need research and development desperately because that is where we can provide the jobs for the future. We cannot continue to bicker among ourselves because if we continue to do so the young people of this nation are going to lose trust in their governments, not only federal but the provincial and other governments of this nation, which do not seem to be providing the will for action. They are not writing the chapters which have to be written in this country so there will be some feeling among our young people that there is a positive future for them, that they can be secure and will get jobs and be able to build a home and have a family. They must have hope that they will enjoy this country because we have everything we need here. All we need is the ability of our institutions to work together to solve the problems. We must get rid of the constant spirit of confrontation which has been in place since this Prime Minister has taken over control of government.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, with all my heart that this must be the final chapter. This Speech from the Throne must be the final chapter of this Government because that is, to my mind, the only way the people of this nation will again have trust in their leadership, the ability to believe that what is said in the Speech from the Throne will in fact be the case. We must carry out the kind of scrutiny of government expenditures which are put in place. We must have the kinds of far-reaching and visionary policy needed to move us toward the 21st century.
One thing a nation must never forget is that all the strong nations of this world must have a sound and strong agricultural base. If one has not the ability to feed oneself, there is not the ability to feed oneself, there is not the ability to grow in any fashion. We are very fortunate in Canada because we have a strong agricultural base. I look at the Speech from the Throne because I am worried about it. We have huge statistics of bankruptcies. The amount of capital which farmers have had to borrow in the last five or six years just to stay alive is horrendous. We are now $18 billion in debt in the agricultural area of this country, at huge interest rates. People involved in agriculture in this country are decreasing in numbers. The small rural communities of this country are in the desperate throes of dying because people are moving away from those areas. There is nothing to keep these people there any more. I look at the Speech from the Throne to see if there are the kinds of far-reaching policies in agriculture to give some confidence to the people and I see mention of a few lofty ideals and some mention of things which ought to have been done years ago, as far as stabilization and advanced payments are concerned. I look forward to seeing if there will be any action on these lofty statements. If there is, we will pass those Bills very quickly, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to participate in this Throne Speech debate because I, as a Minister of the Crown, am very excited about the offering given by the Governor General last week in the Senate. The Throne Speech is exciting. It is dynamic and offers Canadians a program which will help lead us into the next century.
I would like to dwell upon one of the five themes which were raised in the Throne Speech, namely, to reinforce Canada's identity through enhanced recognition of our cultural heritage and increase support for our creative artists by new broadcasting, telecommunications and copyright policies. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, I will be dealing with the former part of that paragraph. As the Throne Speech states:
Wc Canadians know that our diversity-our lack of pressure to conform to a single mold-is an integral part of our identity. Canadian variety, tolerance and civility are to be treasured and nurtured.
As Minister of State for Multiculuralism I feel compelled to underline to Hon. Members of the House of Commons and to the public in general that for the first time a Throne Speech has had a whole paragraph of six substantive items directed to the multicultural nature of this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You have been there for 20 years. It took you a long time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) tells us it took a long time. Well, let us talk about that, Mr. Speaker. It was in 1971 that this Government, under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), introduced the policy of multiculturalism. It has been one of the great Canadian success stories. It has been emulated by provincial governments across this country. It has been emulated by foreign governments. Australia is one. I met with a group of Swedish parliamentarians about two months ago who were looking at the unique social experience which we are undergoing in this country with multiculturalism. The eyes of the world are on Canada for the unique nature of its cultural policies.
In the Throne Speech, Mr. Speaker, we pledged to introduce for the first time a legislative base for multiculturalism. I must admit it is to my regret that this was not done before, but with the exigencies of parliamentary debate and the issues of the day, unfortunately this matter has not been dealt with in terms of establishing a legislative base for multiculturalism. However, as I mentioned, the policy was introduced in 1971. The first Minister was appointed by the Prime Minister in 1974. The new policy expanded beyond the initial one of cultural and linguistic heritage retention to that of social justice and equity under my colleague, the former Minister, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Fleming), who took the lead in developing the new areas dealing with discrimination and racism.
As a result, the House of Commons agreed to the establishment of a Parliamentary Committee on Visible Minorities. We have seen this new direction established in the last two or three
years. We have seen the entrenchment of the principle of multiculturalism in the Constitution, in Article XXVII of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The next step will be taken by this House, hopefully with unanimity, in the legislation I propose to introduce in the House early in the new year. It will incorporate those programs which have had the legislative authority of the Secretary of State's Act since 1971.
I will mention some of them so that people realize the breadth and diversity of the programs. Race relations, of course, is extremely important. Cultural integration, cultural enrichment, group development, writing and publications, Canadian ethnic studies, intercultural communications and performing and visual arts. All of those programs will incorporated in the legislative base we plan to bring forward early in the new year.
In the Throne Speech, Mr. Speaker, we have built on that to re-emphasize and rededicate ourselves to our ethnic heritage and language programs. I should point out that those federal Government programs, and there are about 1,000 of them, involve 125,000 students across this country. The federal Government has led the way. It has not been easy because it must be remembered that we do not have jurisdiction over education. We must co-operate with the provinces and, to give credit where it is due, many of the provinces have given assistance of their own. Some, such as Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Quebec, have done this in the public school system during school hours; others, such as Ontario, have provided funds for after school hours. But it was the federal Government that led the way and I want to emphasize the Throne Speech commitment to rededicate ourselves to that particular approach. We would like to enhance it and I look forward to new developments in the next year or two. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, it is quite possible to encourage the development of other languages in our country in the context of both official languages. It must be emphasized that it was a multicultural group called "Manitoba 23" that strove for the protection of Franco-Manitobans' rights. And their success appears as one of the great triumphs of multicultural policies in Canada.

There were people who said ten or fifteen years ago that we could not move toward a multicultural society, even though the country was in reality becoming a multicultural society, because this would impinge upon the integrity of the official languages of English and French. This was a legitimate intellectual argument, and it is to the credit of the Prime Minister and the Government in 1971 that they took note of this argument but disregarded it. They felt that multiculturalism, as we moved to a multicultural society, in itself would afford perhaps one of the ultimate protections for minority language rights in this country.
What has happened in Manitoba in the last few months is a testament to the wisdom to this kind of reasoning. It was Manitoba 23, an umbrella group of multicultural organiza-
December 14, 1983

tions, which was the most vigorous in defending French-speaking rights for Franco-Manitobans and for articulating that point of view. We see across the country a commonality between all language groups, even the two official languages.
As the Hon. Member for York West said earlier this afternoon, multiculturalism is becoming truly mainstream. Ten years from now we will not be thinking of multiculturalism as "over there"; it will be all of Canada. It will not impinge upon the integrity of the Official Languages Act because the unique nature of this country has been entrenched in the Constitution, and there will be no threat to the growing development of multiculturalism in this country.
Another significant initiative taken in the Throne Speech, Mr. Speaker, comes from the urgings of many of my colleagues on this side of the House. My colleague, the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal), agreed that the representations should be heeded, and that most of the formal requirements for citizenship of a person over 65 will be relaxed. I cannot give a starting date but I am hopeful that we can put this into effect early in the new year.
It is a tragedy when many older people come to this country to join their sons and daughters and they do not have a command of English or French. They go to the Citizenship court and just find it impossible to meet most of the formal requirements for becoming a citizen in answering the questions posed by the judges. This is no reflection on those judges who do an outstanding job, but it is recognition of the fact that there are many people who just cannot meet those basic requirements. They are told by the judge to come back in three months and try again and perhaps they will succeed. This is being said to a 70 or 75 year old person who does not speak English or French and never will. They give up. They say they really want to become a Canadian, their children are here, they belong here, but they just cannot meet these requirements. Well, this Government has taken a very compassionate and humane approach in proposing that most of the formal requirements for those people over 65 will be relaxed in the next short while.
Another significant development in the commitment to multiculturalism also comes, not specifically under my auspices but really under those of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres). It is a commitment by the Government to establish a joint House of Commons and Senate task force on the question of the tax status of charitable foundations and charities. This has a particular impact on the multicultural community since the laws as they are now preclude many of the legitimate activities of multicultural organizations because a charitable tax status number cannot be granted. It is a credit to the Government that we will be asking Members of this House and the Senate to come forward quickly with recommendations on how to improve that situation. This will have an impact on many organizations, but of course I am particularly concerned with those in the multicultural community.
I mentioned earlier this Government's commitment to social justice and equity, and to fight with increasing vigilance to end discrimination and racism in this country. That is the reason
The Address-Mr. Collenette
we came to the House of Commons and sought consent of Members to establish the parliamentary committee. We gained unanimous support, the committee is now working and will be reporting early in the new year. The Government has given its commitment in the Throne Speech that it will be responding as quickly as possible to the recommendations of that very eminent committee.
My colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan), has on a number of occasions reiterated the fact that the Criminal Code as applies to hate literature is woefully inadequate. We have had many discussions on this and they are not yet complete. They will not be complete because we believe new information and recommendations may emanate from the parliamentary committee in this particular area. We do not want to move without having the full weight of the parliamentary committee report. But there is a commitment that the issue of hate literature and its dissemination will be dealt with in this session of Parliament. I think all Canadians welcome that particular measure.
There it is, Mr. Speaker. I believe I have covered everything. We have six points in the Throne Speech which deal with multiculturalism. That reaffirms the commitment of this Government to enhance the development of a truly multicultural society within the context of the two official languages. All Canadians, irrespective of their origin or their background, will feel that their cultural heritage has a true place in this nation.
There was mention in the Speech from the Throne of the great contribution made by immigrants to Canadian society. I feel particularly close to that contribution, being an immigrant myself many years ago along with my family.
When we talk about multiculturalism, we are not just talking about immigrants. We are also talking about their sons and daughters, grandsons and granddaughters. This country was built upon immigration and it is not unusual to find, whether in Metro Toronto, Ontario or western Canada in particular, the sons and daughters and grandsons and granddaughters of the pioneers who came to this country in the nineteenth century maintaining their linguistic heritage and cultural traditions. The continuation of those cultural traditions adds to all of Canadian society.
The maintenance of linguistic traditions is not only beneficial in an intellectual or philosophical sense, it is also beneficial in a purely businesslike, economic sense. As the world becomes more interdependent and as our ties with other countries become even closer through trade, the ability for Canadians to speak other languages, whether it is German where there is a heavy component in the petrochemical and plastics industry, or Chinese and Japanese with respect to trade with the orient, is of great assistance in doing business with countries of the world. All of these languages will add to and have significant benefit for the economic and social wellbeing of the country.

December 14, 1983
The Address-Mr. Collenette
As a new Minister in the Government, I am particularly happy to have been able to make representations to my colleagues and have them accept and bring forward this package. While some may consider it modest, I consider it significant. Indeed, the reaction I have received from the multicultural communities has been that it is significant.
This is the first major commitment to multiculturalism in the Throne Speech since the policy was formulated in 1971. For the first time Parliament will be asked in the New Year to have a full-scale debate on the philosophy of multiculturalism. I will be listening to Hon. Members in this debate and hopefully at committee stage there will be many representations made by ethnocultural organizations in the country. We want to hear from all groups in society. This is one area where there is a consensus and I am sure there will be no parliamentary bickering or division. As a country, we stand to benefit from the advance toward becoming a truly multicultural society.

As the Hon. Minister said, it is very difficult for these people to become citizens and, indeed, it is not just the recent arrivals in Canada. There are people in my riding, especially women, who have been in Canada for up to 25 years. However, because of their cultural heritage they have tended to stay at home and not learn the language, although for all intents and purposes they have been Canadians for 20 or 25 years. These people are now in their early 60s. I hope that we could move quickly with this legislation.
In addition, is there any possibility for the relaxation of the constraints on women in the category I just mentioned who are not yet 65 years of age? Mr. Speaker, I welcome the intervention of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). There are very few Members who are quite as active as he in the multicultural community in the nation's capital.
Perhaps I could approach the issue from this angle: I would be interested in hearing the views of Members on both sides of the House on making the commitment to relax the formal requirements for citizenship for those over 65, which is a basic departure from Government policy. People over the age of 65 are beyond that. I realize that 65 is an arbitrary age but one must start somewhere. I suggest that it is a realistic age from where we must start. We are not talking about legislation here but a regulatory change under the Citizenship Act. I stand to be corrected by my colleague, the Secretary of State, but it is my understanding that that regulation change can be implemented very quickly. For that reason I hope we can move on this early in the new year. Of course, we must give the required time for Citizenship court judges and related administrative matters to be accommodated for that regulatory change.

Mr. Speaker, it is with mixed feelings that 1 once again rise in this House to participate in a debate on the Throne Speech. I have mixed feelings because on the one hand the Speech from the Throne is meant to give Canadians an opportunity to know what the intentions of the Government are in the next sitting of Parliament. It is sometimes an indication of good and perhaps bad things to come. On the other hand, if one looks at the Liberal record of promises outlined in past Throne Speeches, one has to take this Throne Speech with a grain of salt.
I have been in this House now for over ten years. The first time I participated in a debate on a Speech from the Throne I was indeed very excited about all the things outlined in a Liberal Throne Speech. I stood up in this House and accepted some of the tremendous promises outlined in that Liberal Throne Speech in 1972, only to be dismayed, disappointed and disheartened because 99 per cent of the promises made in that and in subsequent Throne Speeches were not kept.
Very quickly one has to look at the record in the last Throne Speech of three and a half years ago, a record time, certainly giving the Government enough time to implement the programs promised. In the 1980 Speech from the Throne the Liberals promised to:
-develop economic policies that will provide jobs, spur growth, improve regional balance and promote Canadian ownership and control of the economy.
Canada has experienced the worst depression since the Great Depression. The November, 1981 Budget drove a faltering economy into a tailspin and Canada's general economic performance dropped to twelfth out of 12 OECD countries.
The 1980 Throne Speech also said:
-continue the policies of expenditure restraint... reduce the deficit in a planned and orderly manner.
We all know that the deficit has risen from $12.6 billion to over $31 billion. Just this week the Auditor General tells us that the Government is hiding billions more dollars. I could list dozens and dozens more specific promises made three and a half years ago, none of which was kept. How can we even debate this Throne Speech with any sense of seriousness when the record speaks for itself, Mr. Speaker? If the Government would bring in programs in the form of legislation that are positive and realistic, we on this side of the House would support them.
There are some suggestions in that speech that would be supported by this Party. For instance, the commitment to world peace. Who is not in favour of world peace? We have been talking about it for years. I have been talking about it ever since I escaped from communist Czechoslovakia in 1948.

Never use government money as a basis for making a business decision; stay away from them if you are thinking that way; do not go near them. It is better to get out of business than to get stuck with those guys.
Those were the comments of Mr. Bulloch who has over
65,000	small businessmen in his organization. I agree with those words. The thrust of government in small business must be to lay back and open a free environment for the worker to work in. It should have incentives available, if necessary, and when my Party takes office it will follow that thrust.
We are working on specific policies which will reduce government bureaucracy and interference in the small business sector. We in the Progressive Conservative Party have long recognized the importance of small business to the Canadian economy, as well as the importance of the entrepreneur, the risk taker or the guy who sweats and mortgages his house to produce materials for sale. He pays taxes, but what happens to him? He is penalized if he is successful rather than being rewarded.
The entire tax system must be overhauled in order to allow small and medium-sized businessmen to get out from under the smothering system the Liberal Government has placed upon their shoulders in the last 10 years to 15 years. It must be replaced with incentive programs, whether they be employment incentives or incentives for research and development. The Liberal administration has been promising increases in research and development for 15 years, yet we are one of the lowest nations in the world in terms of providing research and development for the private sector, the public sector or any other sector, with respect to the Gross National Product. Reduction of government regulations and government spending restraints are other areas. I wish I had more time to elaborate on them.
This week the Auditor General came down with his report. It resulted in the following headlines: "Watchdog says Ottawa's books misleading by billions of dollars"; "Government 'lacks will' to cut waste"; "Govt, spent $4 million on empty office building"; "Waste costs taxpayers a bundle"; and the list continues.
